messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marina, a 43-year-old chef of European background who had been in a long-term relationship, first understood the illness as something routine. It began with abdominal pain that seemed stubborn but ordinary, then a sudden deterioration that left her in the hospital hearing words she had never expected to hear about her own body: life-threatening, emergency surgery, complications. What stayed with her was not only the fear of dying but the helplessness of being watched over, cut open, and dependent on strangers while her body betrayed her. Afterward, she could not hold the experience in mind as a finished event. When the memory returned, it did so with full force, complete and sensory, as if the fluorescent lights, antiseptic smell, beeping monitors, and sharp edge of pain had all crowded back in at once. At those moments Marina was overwhelmed by grief for the version of herself she believed had been lost.

In the months that followed, Marina came to believe that her body had been permanently damaged by what happened, and that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again. Those beliefs shaped the way she moved through daily life. She watched her own body for signs of weakness, convinced that every tightening in her chest or flutter of nausea meant danger was returning, and she could not relax even in her own apartment or in the quiet of the kitchen at work. She also struggled with the sense that the whole event was so extreme it hardly seemed possible that it had happened to her at all; parts of it felt unreal, as if she were recalling a story told by someone else. Yet that distance did not protect her. The more she thought about the hospital stay, the more the images and bodily sensations broke through, and the more certain she became that her body remained an enemy that could turn on her without warning. Those appraisals made her scanning and alarm more intense, so that a small wave of tiredness or a passing ache could pull her back into fear almost before she had time to think.

That alarm soon began to shape her behavior. Marina started numbing her feelings because any sustained attention to what she had survived seemed to crack open grief she could not bear. She avoided situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful, because hope felt dangerous to her now; if she allowed herself to imagine being well again, she feared the fall would be unbearable if symptoms returned. She also began staying up until very late, stretching the day out as long as possible, partly because sleep meant vulnerability and partly because she dreaded lying still with her thoughts. These habits brought short-term relief, but they also left her more exhausted and disconnected, and that emotional flatness made it harder for her to feel anchored in the present. The more she numbed herself and pushed away anything uplifting, the more convinced she became that something essential in her had gone missing and that she was no longer capable of ordinary feeling. That belief fed back into her withdrawal, making the world seem smaller and less safe.

The threat reactions never stayed quiet for long. In the kitchen at work, where the heat, metallic smells, and sudden demands already kept everyone on edge, Marina would sometimes be seized by a jolt of certainty that danger was happening again. Her body reacted before her mind could catch up; a change in sensation, a momentary pain, or the sight of a tray of medical-looking tubing in a television image could make her feel as if she were back in the hospital, trapped inside the same helplessness. At such times the memory returned not as a thought but as an embodied reliving, and the more vivid it became, the more she concluded that her body was still damaged and unreliable. That conviction made the alarms feel justified. If her body could betray her once, she reasoned, then every physical cue might be the first sign of catastrophe, and every flashback or wave of panic only confirmed that she was still in danger. In turn, she numbed herself more deeply, avoided anything that might brighten her mood, and stayed up late to postpone the quieter hours when the images would rise.

What finally brought Marina to seek help was the growing sense that she was no longer managing her life so much as arranging it around fear. Her partner had begun noticing how often she seemed distant, how little joy she allowed herself, and how frequently she startled or went rigid at ordinary sensations. Marina was afraid that she would remain trapped in this state indefinitely, unable to trust her own body or her own emotions, and she was beginning to worry that the grief, the sleeplessness, and the constant internal vigilance were costing her both her relationship and her work. What she hoped for was simpler and more fragile: to feel safe in her own skin again, and to believe that feeling alive would not necessarily mean being hurt all over again.
